en: From the time of the initiation ceremony (upanayana) onwards, he should observe the vows: 1.
wearing clothes made of deerskin; 2. keeping his hair matted.
4. His livelihood shall consist of begging and acting as a teacher. 5. He shall carry a staff made of bamboo with its bark intact. 6. He shall wear a girdle made of seven strands of muñja grass.
He shall not eat honey or meat; he shall avoid alkaline substances and salt; he shall not act contrary to his teacher.
He is not independent in any of his affairs;
he should rise before [his teacher] and go to bed after him;
whatever he might obtain, that he should give to him.
One should not share a bed with many people, nor should one mount a chariot [with many]. 13–15.
He should not dress [inappropriately]; 16 he should avoid all tactile contact with women; 17 he should not look at a woman who is naked; 18.
One should not speak for the sake of dwelling; 19 one should not retain anything for the sake of pleasure; 20 one should not bathe. 21
Or he should enter the water;
if he bathes, he should float in the water like a staff.
He may be shaven-headed, wear matted hair, or have a topknot.
One should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) both in the evening and in the morning;
one should stand during the former and sit during the latter.
Having uttered "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ," he recites the Sāvitrī verse beginning with "tatsavitur.
(28) Having gone out before sunset, he should fetch fuel-sticks that are greenish-yellow if he desires Vedic luster; so says the Śruti.
(29) [These duties include] the performance of the morning and evening Sandhyā prayers, going out for alms, and tending the sacred fire. (30)
Some say that he should kindle the fire only in the evening.
(31) There is a fault in failing to go for alms and in failing to kindle the fire; having failed to do this for seven nights, one should perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin*.

(32) Having worshipped the fire with the section beginning "Thou art the pervader" (*vibhūrasi*), he places a fuel-stick on it with the formula "Thou art fuel" (*edho 'si*); a second with "Thou art a fuel-stick" (*samidasi*); a third with "This I [place] in the fire" (*idamaham agnau*); and a fourth with "This I [place] in the fire" (*idamaham agnau*). (1)
He consecrates the fire with the mantra, "Thou art splendor," and worships himself with the remainder of the formula, "Bestow splendor upon me. 2. Then, in the morning before sunrise—3.

He who practices studentship for twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six, or forty-eight years, even if he becomes dirty, weak, and emaciated, obtains everything after his bath; whatever he desires in his mind, he attains through this very discipline; thus one studies well according to this dharma. 4.
Having understood the meanings of the Vedic hymns (*chandas*), one who intends to perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) should cause a cow to be given as a gift and honor the teacher.
(1) A *śrotriya* is one other than the student who has mastered the Vedas; (2) for such a person, there is no [obligatory] ritual bath. (3)

Now follows his bath: having caused him to put on a garment from Vraja, he should have his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails removed. Then he should bathe with the three verses beginning with "The waters indeed," and with the two verses beginning with "Golden-colored. "Golden-colored, purifying, in whom Kaśyapa was born, in whom Indra, those who, being of various forms, have held Agni as their embryo—may those waters be auspicious and pleasant for us. Golden-colored, purifying, they have moved forth, leaving behind all that is blameworthy; the waters have spread out a hundred purifiers. With them may the god Savitṛ purify me. And [he should bathe] with the two verses beginning with "Auspicious for us. (4–5)
With the words, "May heaven be thy back," he should hold up a parasol;
with "O Agni," gold;
and with the words, "Ye two are supports, O divine ones, do not harm me," he puts on shoes made of boar-skin.
From this point forward, he shall wear two garments; therefore, according to the Śruti, beautiful clothing must be worn.
He shall always carry a bamboo staff, hold an umbrella, and yield the path to others.
Taking what is not given is forbidden (12);
departing by a side door (13);
conversing with a woman in her menstrual period (14).
15. Sleeping on the same bed as one wearing dusty clothes;
16. Speaking harsh words to one's guru;
17. Laughing, running, singing, dancing, and looking at such [behaviors] in an inappropriate place.

Now, therefore, follows the [section] consisting of forty-eight [sections]: 1. Therein, the specific rule is as follows: 2. In regard to the observances (niyamas), the teacher shall be the primary authority. 3.
One seeking a dwelling should not enter that which is occupied by a youth;
one should remain without a fixed abode,
except for a tree or an anthill.
Some say it should be free from animal hair;
as it has been stated, there should be a single garment made of hemp or wool; its measured width across the chest should reach above the knees.
He may eat food and drink at the fourth meal-time;
he should not accumulate possessions; or he may eat almsfood day after day.
He should remain standing during the day and sit at night;
he should observe both [these postures] as a vow of a sage (muni).
One should not converse with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who are impulsive, or those who are menstruating—so says Cyavana Bhṛgu.
Or for twelve nights on both occasions— namely,
the new moon and the full moon.
The fuel sticks are always made of *pālāśa* wood, or from the trees prescribed for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

Having given the "hand-path" with the mantra, "May wisdom come to me," one should perform the ritual bathing in water at the three daily junctures (triṣavaṇa) throughout the day and night. (19) At each juncture, one should recite: "Homage to Hamāya, to Mohamāya; homage to Agni Vaiśvānara, to Tapas, to Tāpasa, to Tapanta, to Vindu, to Vinda, to Vasuvinda, to Sarvavinda; homage to Pāra, to Supāra, to Pārayant; homage to Ūrmya, to Sūrmya; homage to Cyavana Bhārgava. One should thus satiate these very deities with water.
(20) Having performed this for a year, he becomes stainless and free from sin. (21)

If one who has completed his student life (*brahmacarya*) does nothing else, he indeed, having completed his student life, purifies ten descendants and ten ancestors; he purifies himself as the twenty-first, and also the line of people as far as he can see sitting in it, for whomsoever he sits.
When [the meal] is finished, he offers oblations of food to these very deities.
A cow is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 25.
We shall explain the procedure for the Kṛcchra penance:
1. Just as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Aṅgirases practiced it in ancient times, O gods. 2.
He should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra; he should sit down at night seeking shelter;
and he should remain standing throughout all the days.
6. A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should sleep at night; 7. he should avoid honey, meat, salt, and offerings made to the ancestors (śrāddha), without hesitation;
8. the skin of a cow, linen, bark-cloth, wool, or deerskin are said to be [suitable] garments.
Even the Maruts practiced in this way for the sake of liberation from all unwholesome states.

(10) For three days one should eat in the evening, for three days in the morning, and for three days one should eat food that has not been asked for; for three days, however, one should not eat at all—this is the vow practiced by the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. (11) This very rule is prescribed as the procedure for the Atikṛcchra penance. (12)
During these very times, one should consume only a single morsel of food each day.
13. We shall now explain the *taptakṛcchra* (the hot penance):

for three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk; for three days one should drink hot clarified butter; and for the final three days, one should subsist on air alone. 2.
This same rule is prescribed for the *kūrca* penance of Bṛhaspati:

one should consume gruel, barley-meal, vegetables, milk, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass for three days each; then for the final three days, one should subsist on air alone. Next is the *sāntapana*.
The oblation to the Maruts shall satisfy the Maruts.

Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass, together with a fast for one night, is known as the *Sāntapana* penance. This same [set of substances] practiced three times is known as the *Mahāsāntapana*.

Now, regarding the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*): having taken up the vow with the formula, "The Vasus are the lords of the vow; the Rudras are the lords of the vow; the Ādityas are the lords of the vow; the Maruts and Aṅgirases are the lords of the vow," he should satisfy the Vasus with water during the first three-night period, the Rudras in the second, the Ādityas in the third, and the Maruts and Aṅgirases in the fourth. With the two verses beginning "Come to my house" (*ā me gṛhā*), he offers oblations of the *sthālīpāka* belonging to the Vasus.
With the verse beginning "asaṅkhyātā" (ten times), he offers to the Rudras;
with the five verses beginning "kadā cana starīrasi" (five times), to the Ādityas;

with the six verses beginning "sāntapanāḥ" (six times), to the hosts of Maruts; and with the two verses beginning "tvām agne aṅgirasaḥ" and "vāyur agregāḥ" (six times); and with the verse beginning "havyavāham" (seven times), he offers to Sviṣṭakṛt.

During the rainy season, he performs the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) of the Vedic lessons under the asterism Śravaṇa. He offers oblations with the following verses: "Thou art named *Apvā*; may I go unto thy favor; for from my father indeed have I received the wisdom of the *ṛta*, and I have become like Sūrya—*svāhā*! The three subsequent [verses] are: "Thou art named *Ranti*, thou art named *Yukti*, thou art named *Yoga*. To each of these, he appends the phrase "may I go unto thy favor" (*tasyāste juṣṭīyaṃ gameyam*). Desiring the acquisition of knowledge for his pupils, he offers at the end: "*Svāhā* to *Yuj*, *svāhā* to *Udyuj*, *svāhā* to *Yukti*, *svāhā* to *Yoga*!"

Having consumed curd three times with the verse "O Dadhikrāvan," he, holding *darbha* grass in his hand, recites the *Sāvitrī* three times, as well as the first three *anuvākas*, and [the hymn] beginning with "Who yokes you? (RV 10.13). 4.
For this [period], there is no study. 5.
There is no study when lightning is flashing or when it is thundering. 6.
7. Untimely thunderous celestial noise, lightning, clouds, and meteors; 8. Others [suffer] through improper conduct; 9. Indistinct sounds and a continuous flow of urine with drops.

Having studied for four and a half months, or five and a half months, they dismiss [the students] with the words, "We dismiss the lessons; may the Vedic meters trust us again," and with the verse, "Who releases you? (RV 8.43.31).
There is no study on that new-moon day, nor does he study during the "bird-day" (the two days surrounding the new moon). After this, there is no study when clouds appear.
Now, those worthy of the Upaniṣads:

a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), one of good conduct, one who is intelligent, one who performs his duties, a giver of wealth, a friend, or one seeking knowledge through [the means of] knowledge—these are the *tīrthas* for attaining Brahman. In a new dwelling site that is level, provided with roots, and well-drained—or having leveled it so that water flows away toward the northeast or the north-west—one should have a shelter constructed there with a door facing either east or south.

Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward for the builder of the middle [post], he places the pillar upon it: "I fix you, the steadfast one, the consort of immortality; stand firm in security, dripping with ghee. O pillar, may we dwell here together with you—possessing all heroes, possessing good heroes, and possessing unharmed heroes. Right here, O pillar, grow with immortality, rich in horses, rich in cattle, rich in immortality, rich in pleasant truth, full of vigor, and full of milk. O pillar, turn toward us with milk."
"May the young boy come to you; may the calf come with the moving world; may the jar of *parisrut* come to you; may this one [come] with the vessels of curd.

(2) He erects the bamboo beam facing eastward with: "By means of Truth, ascend the pillar, O beam; being fierce and radiant, drive away the enemies. Then may we, possessing all heroes, [attain] wealth.
(3) This is the northern-eastern placement. (4)

Having sacrificed with the four verses beginning "O Vāstoṣpati, the remover of disease," from the *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Vāstoṣpati, he may then enter the dwelling: "O Vāstoṣpati, removing disease, entering all forms, be a kind friend to us. O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us; be easy of access and free from disease for us. Since we approach you, accept that from us; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds. O Vāstoṣpati, be our furtherer; increase our household with cattle and horses, O Indu."

"May we be free from old age in your friendship; be gracious toward us as a father toward his sons. O Vāstoṣpati, may we dwell in your auspicious and delightful abode that provides a path. Protect our welfare both in rest and in exertion. And do you all protect us always with blessings. (RV 7.54.1) 1. One should feed Brāhmaṇas for the inspection of the lineage. 2.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Gṛhyapañcikā on the Laugākṣi-sūtra.
Now follows the *pākayajña*.
The *pākayajña* is of four kinds: the *huta*, the *ahuta*, the *prahuta*, and the *prāśita*. Of these, the *huta* belongs to the [category of] *huta* offerings.
The *upahāra* is for those [offerings] not formally sacrificed (*ahuta*);
the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is for those formally sacrificed (*prahuta*);
and the *madhuparka* and *brahmaudana* are for those consumed (*prāśita*).
The *pākayajñas* have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as their archetype (7). In those [sacrifices], the procedure is performed silently (8),
except for that which is not omitted by its purpose (9).
And because of the absence of the *prayāja* offerings, there is no *upabhṛt* ladle.
One should marry during the northern course of the sun; one should choose a bride among those born under the asterisms of Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, or Pūrva-phalgunī.
One should examine the characteristics by means of the characteristic marks (3).
Or one may examine the fortune by means of lumps of earth (4).

Earth should be collected from a sacrificial altar, a furrow, a pool, a cow-pen, a gambling place, a burning ground, a crossroads, and a barren spot; the ninth [type] is that which is brought together from all these (5).

"Truth alone is the Supreme; nothing transcends Truth. Upon Truth this earth rests—this [earth] and that [heaven]. Having spoken thus, and having taken into his hand the balls of food marked on all sides, he should present them to the maiden while pronouncing her name: "May she become this.
He should say, "Take one of these.
If she takes one of the first four, he should marry her.
Some say it may also be performed during the *saṃbhārya* [period]. 9.
For the wedding ceremony (*upayama*), one should choose the asterisms Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Śraviṣṭhā, or the Uttarās. 10.
Or rather, that which is declared auspicious [by the astrologers]. 11.

Now we shall describe the procedure for the gift of a *brahmadeyā* (a bride given as a religious gift). 1. On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, or on a festival day, having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing north, the recipient sits facing east together with his attendants, and the giver sits facing west. 2.

Having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing east in the middle [between them] and its tips pointing north, and having placed water upon it and scattered rice and barley, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), seated to the south facing north, should cause the taking up of the supporting vessel (*upayamana*). 3.
When they have assembled, he says three times, "I give," and "I accept.

Having said, "This is the truth for you," the officiating priest (ṛtvij), looking at both [the bridegroom and the bride], mutters the verses: "United be your [hearts]," and "United be your minds. Now follows the procedure regarding the gift to be given.
He exchanges gold [with the words], "For offspring thee" (2); he gives it away with, "For the increase of wealth thee" (3);
he receives it with, "For the increase of wealth thee" (4).
Having poured gold into a bronze vessel, they touch it together with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ."

Having adorned the girl with Gaudānika mantras, while she sits facing east on a four-legged auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), four women who are not widows, her mother, her father, and the Guru as the seventh, having bathed her with a purifier (pavitra) of a thousand holes, and having covered her with a new garment, he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* [sacrificial porridge] with the formula: "To Indra, Svāhā! To Indrāṇī, Svāhā! To Kāma, Svāhā! To Bhaga, Svāhā! To Hrī, Svāhā! To Śrī, Svāhā! To Lakṣmī, Svāhā! To Puṣṭi, Svāhā! To Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas, Svāhā! (1)

Having smeared with scented water the flute, the *tūṇava* drum, the *mṛdaṅga* drum, the *paṇava* drum, and all musical instruments, the girl plays them, saying: "Speak aloud, O drum; for the sake of good offspring, O *gomukha* drum! Let the girls play, being well-disposed and having performed the auspicious rites together with Indra's consort.
(2) She plays with each friend for one day, or for two days and nights.
(3) Having covered a branch of a sacrificial tree that extends eastward and has been cut in a single stroke with a thread, he gives it to the girl with a verse addressed to Savitṛ. (1)

"Whatever misfortune you have—whether derived from your mother, derived from your father, transmissible, or even innate—that I banish along with the deity Tiṣya; I drive it away. Let it go to the enemy. Homage, homage to Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati!
(2) Its disposal is in stagnant water, in pure water, or in a sanctuary of the gods.
(3) Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *haviṣya* (sacrificial food). (1)

For maidens, the period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is ten years, or twelve years. At the conclusion of the period of celibacy, having kindled two fires—the Gandharva fire and the Devakula fire—he dedicates two animals: the southern one for Aryaman and the northern one for Prajāpati. In the event that this is not possible, however, there is only a single animal.
Or one may perform [the sacrifice] with rice grains. The ribs should be placed in their proper positions, and the portions for cutting (avadānas) likewise; so too the sacrificial oblation (havis).

One should worship Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Skanda, Rudra, Vātsīputra, Bhaga, the Bhaga-nakṣatras, Kālī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Bhadrakālī, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Mahiṣikā with offerings of fragrant substances.
Now, therefore, follows the auspicious day for the oblation (haviṣyapuṇyāha).

Having gone to the edge of water, or having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in milk as available, and having bathed her including her head with all kinds of perfumes ending with fruits, and having covered her with a new garment, he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* to Indra’s wife, Varuṇa’s wife, Gandharva’s wife, the Waters, Agni Jīvaputra, Prajāpati Mahārāja, Skanda, Aryaman, Bhaga, and Prajanaka.

On the very second night when he is about to marry the girl, after that night has passed, he should fetch a new pot, cook a *sthālīpāka* (pot-boiling) in milk, bathe her together with her head while she wears it, using all kinds of perfumes and ending with fruits, and cover her with a new garment; then he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Udarka, Bhaga, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and King Prajāpati.
For a male child, he should sacrifice to these same deities, as well as to Vaiśravaṇa and Īśāna.

Four or eight widows, having fed Brāhmaṇas with balls of vegetables and food, should sing together with lute-players; or else, four [widows] should perform a dance. [They should sing: "Sing forth to your sportive host of Maruts, the unassailable, the chariot-rulers," O Kaṇvas!

He should sacrifice fried barley-meal to Agni Puṣṭipati and Prajāpati, [reciting the verses]: "Through Agni may he obtain wealth and nourishment day by day, glorious and most rich in heroes," and "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you."
In all marriage rites where no specific deity has been prescribed, one should sacrifice to Agni, the Lord of Prosperity (Puṣṭipati), and Prajāpati.
Now follows the rite for departure (prāsthānika).

Having kindled the fire in that place as previously described and having offered oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, the sister then takes hold of the hem of his garment after he has taken up a weapon.
"Pūṣan, lead us" (RV 6.54.1)—with these words they go to where there is water.
Having touched the water with "The goddesses [be] auspicious to us" (RV 10.9.4), they proceed toward the directions with "The eastern direction... (VS 34.11) according to their respective quarters.
There are six persons worthy of the *arghya* offering: the teacher, the officiating priest, the king, one to be married, a beloved friend, and the *snātaka*.
Then they honor him:
first, at the beginning of the rite,
with the *arghya* water, medicinal herbs, and *darbha* grass.

Having poured curd and honey into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, having covered it with a larger lid, and having grasped it with two mats, they proceed with the rites beginning with the water for the feet (pādya).
5. He consecrates the [water] being brought with the formula: "Thou art the milking in me; thou art the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj for the sake of the water for the feet.
6. Having spread out a mat with the formula, "Thou art a mat; sit upon the mother," he sits down upon it. 7.
To him who is seated on a grass mat, he recites each verse three times.
[The guest] says, "Not so, sir," or "No, friend.

Having consecrated water with the mantra "May the goddesses be auspicious to us," he washes [the guest's feet] with the water for washing the feet, saying: "Wash the right foot; I place Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) in this family. Wash the left foot; I place in myself brilliance, vigor, food, offspring, cattle, and Vedic splendor."

Having taken up the *arghya* water with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he takes the *madhuparka* with the *Sāvitra* formula. Having drawn out the *viṣṭara* grass-bundle with the words, "Thou art a *viṣṭara*; rest upon the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)," and having spread it out with "O wide one (*uru*) thee!," and having looked at it with "That eye of yours...," and having placed it on the *viṣṭara* with "Of the earth thee!," he stirs it clockwise with his forefinger while reciting the three verses beginning with "Honey for the wind, for the one who follows the Law."

"May the Vasus, whose king is Agni, consume you; may the Pitṛs, whose king is Yama, consume you; may the Rudras, whose king is Soma, consume you; may the Ādityas, whose king is Varuṇa, consume you; may the Viśvedevas, whose king is Bṛhaspati, consume you. With these mantras, he wipes away the remnants of the smearings at the edges of the vessel, moving clockwise from direction to direction.
"That which is the supreme form of the honeyed, most excellent food of honey—by that, may I become the supreme eater of honeyed, most excellent food, and one who partakes of honey."

"Thou art the glory of the threefold knowledge; thou art the glory of prosperity; thou art the radiance of the Brahman for the sake of glory; thou art truth-glory, glory, and prosperity. May prosperity rest upon me, may prosperity rest upon me. With these words, he consumes four mouthfuls of the *madhuparka*: first with the little finger, then with the ring finger, then with the middle finger, and finally with the thumb—the second finger being used for each. Having consumed it in this successive order using all the fingers, he gives what remains to a friend.
(13) He sips water with the formula: "Thou art the under-layer for the nectar. (14) Then, with a sword in his hand, he addresses the cow to him. (15)
He instructs her: "Destroy the evil of both myself and this man; my evil is destroyed; destroy my evil—do so, Om!
(16) He should feed four Brahmins of different lineages. (17) This is the first method. (18)

If she should let her go, he should mutter: "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality—I proclaim this to the discerning people: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi! May she be blessed with good pasture; and may we also be blessed. Having said, "Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you wander," and saying, "Om, let her go; eat grass," once she has been released, [he offers] either a bull or a ram. It is known from tradition that there should be no meat in the *madhuparka*; or rather, it may consist of rice cooked in ghee.

Thus ends the second chapter of the Gṛhyapañcikā on the Laugākṣi-sūtra. "May the paths be thornless and straight, by which our friends go to choose a bride. May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; may the lordship over the household be well-governed, O Gods!"—with these words he sends forth the messenger. Having covered [the vessel] with a branch of the *śamī* tree together with its leaves, he should bring it back. 1–2.

One should perform the water-rites with these very waters: "May the waters of the desert be auspicious to us; may the waters of the marshes be auspicious to us; may the waters of the ocean be auspicious to us; may those waters that are here be auspicious to us. With these verses, which are not [mixed] with other waters, he causes her who has bathed to put on an unwashed garment, saying: "The goddesses who cut [the wool], who carded it, who spun it, and the goddesses who gave the ends on both sides—may those goddesses clothe you with old age; O long-lived one, put on this garment! Having caused her to put on the unwashed garment, he girds her from within with a girdle made of muñja grass or of darbha grass, while reciting: "Hoping for longevity... and so forth.

Desiring goodwill, offspring, prosperity, and wealth, being devoted to Agni, I gird myself for the sake of good deeds. I release her from here, not from there; well-bound, yet making her go thither. O bounteous Indra, so that she may be possessed of good sons and be fortunate. May Pūṣan lead her, taking her by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot. Go to the house that you may be mistress of the household; as one who has power, may you prosper in the assembly. May those waylayers who lie in wait find no one; may the couple pass over the difficult path by easy ways; may the enemies flee away. Thus, having led her forth. 4. Desiring goodwill, offspring, prosperity, and wealth, being devoted to Agni, I gird myself for the sake of good deeds. I release her from here, not from there; well-bound, yet making her go thither. O bounteous Indra, so that she may be possessed of good sons and be fortunate. May Pūṣan lead her, taking her by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot. Go to the house that you may be mistress of the household; as one who has power, may you prosper in the assembly. The ritual for the garment has been stated (6). Now follow the customary practices (7): silently producing fire by friction from a hearth, or taking fire that is already burning from outside, one should enkindle the sacred fire, sweep around it, sprinkle water around it, and strew grass around it. Having prepared clarified butter that has been melted and purified, and having offered the oblations from the *āghāra* up to the *ājyabhāga* portions, one should station a chariot or a cart to the west of the fire and yoke it with the mantra, "At every yoking..."—the right one first, the other next, and the left one last. (8)

"Silently releasing [the horse] from the hole of the chariot, the hole of the cart, and the hole of the yoke, O Śatakratu, having sprinkled Apālā with water three times, O Indra, may he make her radiant as the sun"—having thus tied a piece of gold to a *niṣṭarkya* (a small stone) and placed it upon her head at the right-hand hole of the yoke, he pours water over it with the mantra: "May the gold be auspicious for you; may the waters be auspicious; may the wedge be auspicious for you; may the hole of the yoke be auspicious. May the waters, possessing a hundred purifiers, be auspicious for you; unite yourself with this husband in body. To the south stands a man.
Then he offers oblations: "To Agni, the knower of wives, svāhā! To Soma, the knower of wives, svāhā! To Gandharva, the knower of wives, svāhā!
(11) He offers the *santanī* oblations with the formula, "The breath of life" (12), as well as the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations (13).
He offers those presiding powers as prescribed,
with the three verses beginning with "ākūtyā" and ending with "tvā."
With the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," reciting one verse at a time (17);
with the four Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) beginning with "bhūḥ svāhā" (18);
and with the three Agni-Pāvamānī verses beginning with "agna āyūṃṣi" (19).

Having offered oblations repeatedly, he should pour the remnants (saṃpāta) upon the head of the girl with these three [mantras]: "That body of yours which is husband-destroying, I make that body of yours non-husband-destroying; svāhā! That body of yours which is childless, I make that body of yours possessed of children; svāhā! That body of yours which is cattle-less, I make that body of yours possessed of cattle; svāhā! (20)

Having placed the bride facing eastward upon darbha grass to the north of the fire, the pure groom, standing to the east and facing west, takes her hand with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand. He takes her right hand, palm upward, including the thumb, while his own hand is held low and empty; likewise, he takes her left hand with his left hand.

With the words, "I take," he causes the bridegroom to recite four verses: "I take your two hands for the sake of good offspring, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the householdership. O Pūṣan, lead her forward, most auspiciously, she in whom men sow their seed; she who, longing for us, parts her thighs, and in whom we, longing, shall deposit the member. Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni."
"Agni has given me wealth and sons, as well as this woman. Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next; Agni is your third husband; I am the fourth, born of man.
(22) Then he causes him to recite the *anuvāka* beginning with "O Sarasvatī, come hither" (*sarasvati predamava*). According to some, both [the bridegroom and the student] recite it.
(23) If the ritual procedure is separate, having led the fire around clockwise and seated him right there, he should conclude the rite. (24)

In the case of a single ritual (*ekakarma*), having returned to the fire according to the subsequent rule, then follows the marriage ceremony. (25) Those oblations at the wedding beginning with "These two, heaven and earth" (*ya ime dyāvāpṛthivī*), as well as the *jaya* offerings and so forth, do not belong to the single ritual procedure; nor do the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. (26) To the west of the fire, upon *darbha* grass, he causes her to recite: "Thou art she; I am he. She is thou; I am he. Come, let us two marry for the sake of producing a son, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for great heroism. (27)

Having led the bride around the fire from left to right with the words, "Come, step upon the stone," he causes the groom to step upon the stone with his right foot, [reciting]: "Come, step upon the stone; like a stone, may you be firm. May all the gods grant you a life of a hundred autumns. [He says] "Step upon this" to the bride: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm. Crush those who seek to harm us; overcome those who attack us.

(28) Having spread a base of clarified butter in her joined palms, and having touched it with the words, "This is the oblation," then either her brother or a student (*brahmacārī*) pours *śamī* leaves and parched grain (*lāja*) into her hands. (29)

Interruption-free, she offers [the oblations] with the verse, "Now to the god Aryaman... (RV X.85.21): "Now the maiden has worshipped the god Agni; may that god Aryaman release us from the house of that man. *Svāhā!* (30) He causes her to recite, "Agni, the progenitor... (RV X.85.36): "May Agni, the progenitor, make me a progenitor through this woman; may I have a living husband.
(31) She attaches the verse, "This woman... (RV X.85.37), everywhere: "This woman speaks while sowing the young sprouts: 'May my husband live long; may my kinsmen prosper. (32)
In this manner, repeating it twice more—thus three times at each step—he performs an oblation of parched grain (*lājāhoma*) and causes the bridegroom to place both the sacrificial fee and the stone.

"The Gandharva who finds the wife"—with these words, the maiden has worshipped the Gandharva who finds the wife; may that divine Gandharva release us from the house of such-and-such a person, *svāhā*. 35.

He makes her recite: "May Soma make me possessed of kinsmen; through this [rite], may Soma make me possessed of kinsmen; may I be one whose husband lives. (36) "Tryambaka we worship," he says. "Tryambaka we worship, the fragrant, the nourisher of husbands. Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from the houses of that man. Svāhā! (37) He makes her recite: "May Pūṣan make me possessed of cattle; through this [rite], may Pūṣan make me possessed of cattle; may I be one whose husband lives. (38)

He offers the remaining portions to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the winnowing basket; the performer [of the rite] is the sacrificial fee (vara). Having silently released his hands, he unties the binding cord with the mantra, "I unloose for thee."

To the north of the fire, upon darbha grass, he causes her to step forward toward the east: "One for food; two for strength; three for the increase of wealth; four for happiness; five for offspring; six for the seasons; seven for long life. "Be a friend with seven steps, O gracious one, O possessor of wealth; may you not be separated from my sight. "May Viṣṇu follow you"—this is to be supplied [to each verse].
(42) He causes her to worship the sun with the mantra beginning "That eye... (43). When the sun has set, [he causes her to worship] the fire. (44)
"Arundhatī shows Jīvantī, Dhruva, Svastyātreya, and Arundhatī herself. 'Do you see each one of these? he asks; 'I see them,' she replies.
(45) "This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her. Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart for your homes. With these words, he addresses those who have looked at her. (46)

With the verse, "Up to the highest," he addresses her as she goes toward a dwelling in the north-east, or wherever it may be: "Ascending to the highest, casting away those who attack, ascend to the head of your husband and become pre-eminent with offspring. O bountiful Indra, make this woman blessed with good sons and fortunate. Bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh. Be a sovereign lady over your father-in-law; be a sovereign lady over your mother-in-law."

"Be a sovereign lady over your sister-in-law; be a sovereign lady over your brothers-in-law; [be sovereign] over your daughters-in-law, your fathers-in-law, your offspring, and your wealth; be a radiant queen over your husbands, your brothers-in-law, and your kinsmen. With these words, on an auspicious day, he yokes [the cart]. He yokes it with the mantra: "At every union... (RV 10.85.20). He consecrates the two wheels with the mantra: "The two carts that move about the chariot on both sides, those dark ones that fly toward the edge of the wind, the far-reaching, winged, and powerful ones—may those fires, moving forward, carry us across. Those who are called "ford-makers" at the ford—those who are slow-moving—bestow wealth along with heroes upon the eloquent man in the dwelling of humanity. O Lords of the Forest (*vanaspati*), you have made this ford well-measured; strike down the obstacle standing in the path and the evil-minded one. May this Lord of the Forest lead us safely to the further shore of the great [river]. O Sīrā, be easy for us to cross for the sake of long life and splendor. The river flows, full of stones; take hold of it, rise up, and move forward, O friends! Here we leave behind those who were unkind; may we cross over toward auspicious strengths. 12. *Atharvaveda* 6.108.1–3; *Rigveda* 10.53.8–9; *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.4.13.1–3.
With "May there be well-being for us," he crosses a river.

With "He who [rejoins] even that which is broken," when a part of the chariot is shattered: "Even that which is joined together before the joints are pierced, Maghavan, the possessor of many riches, heals the fracture; he restores what was dislocated. (2)

In the afternoon, when the sun is behind the trees, having approached the house, he recites the following upon beholding the house: "Bringing strength, a winner of wealth, wise, joyful, and full of luster, I have come to the house. With a non-terrible, friendly eye, looking upon the houses, may I prolong my life. May we prolong the life of the houses; may the houses extend our lifespan. I enter the well-disposed houses, which do not slay heroes, whose lord is a hero, and which are most gracious."
He spreads a layer of sacrificial grass reaching as far as the bed;
by that path he enters;
he enters the dwelling where the fire has been kindled, provided with water and medicinal herbs.

Under the asterism Rohiṇī, or Mūla, or on another auspicious day as prescribed, having sat upon the hide of a red bull or even upon *darbha* grass, he should offer oblations with the *jaya* formulas and with the verse, "May Agni come first. "May Agni come first among the deities; may he lead her offspring to a full lifespan. May King Varuṇa grant his approval for this, so that this woman may ward off the calamity of losing her sons. Svāhā! May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he release her offspring from the noose of death."

May our mother have her attendance unimpaired while she lives; may she fully experience the joy of seeing her grandson—svāhā! May no terrible thing arise in your house at night; let other weeping women lie down elsewhere than with you. O woman whose son is living, shine forth in the world of your husband, beholding your offspring with a well-disposed mind—svāhā! Let not your suckling boy perish; do not you, with disheveled hair, strike yourself upon your breast.

May Savitṛ protect him as he sucks the breast; may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect him constantly from being uncovered by his garment—svāhā! O Agni, you are the expiation among the gods; whatever harsh body she possesses, destroy it for her—svāhā! O Vāyu, you are the expiation! O Sūrya, you are the expiation! O Candra, you are the expiation! O Viṣṇu, you are the expiation! O Viṣṇu, you are the expiation! O Candra, you are the expiation! O Sūrya, you are the expiation! O Vāyu, you are the expiation!

Having silently prepared the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) and having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati from it, they both eat the remainder. Food indeed is the means of separation; food is remembered as the means of reconciliation. Food is the life-breath of cattle; food is remembered as the supreme physician. With a jewel made of food, with the cord of breath that is speckled, with a knot of truth, I bind together your heart and your mind. May your mind be in harmony with your speech; may your thought be in harmony with your vow.

"Like the wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox, let your mind follow mine alone. Behold me and the sun, and do not set your heart on others. May this *saṃvanana* (conciliatory rite) of the cakravāka birds belong to both me and her.
They observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year, or for twelve nights, six, three, or even one night; then the two lie together.

I beheld you with my mind, you who are observant, born of fervor, manifested through fervor. Bestowing upon me offspring here and wealth here, beget yourself through progeny, O you who desire a son! I beheld you with my mind, meditating, striving for success within your own body. As a young woman, rise up toward me; beget yourself through progeny, O you who desire a son! O Prajāpati, take pleasure in my body; may Tvaṣṭṛ with the gods and Indra with his might [favor us].

"In harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice, may we be mothers of many men. I place the embryo in the plants; I am within all living beings. I have generated offspring upon the earth; I [have generated] sons from women who have not yet borne. Thus do they recite, alternating between the man and the woman. (3) In this very manner, those two desiring offspring unite during her fertile period.
(4) He touches her vulva, saying, "May he make... (5)
"Bhasat" refers to the people above;
"bṛhat" refers to what has been born—
thus [ends] the Garbhādhāna.

In the third month of pregnancy, he performs the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight or on a festival day. Having established the fire as prescribed and offered oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, he causes all the hair of the woman—who is seated facing east on *darbha* grass behind the fire—to be loosened and combed out with the verse: "The parting (*sīmanta*) which your comb has made, or which the razor has shaved away—that beauty among women, O Aśvins, bestow upon her; endow her with manly vigor and heroic power. "Indra made the comb; let it glide along the parting."

"O Agni, give back the wife to her husbands along with offspring; Agni has given back the wife with long life and splendor. May he who is her husband live for a hundred autumns with long life. (2) With this verse, three times, she parts the hair-parting (*sīmanta*) using a porcupine quill that is white at the tip, or a branch of the *śamī* tree together with its leaves, [reciting]: "O Rākā, those [locks] of yours... (3) Then she binds her two separate masses of hair with a blue-and-red thread, [reciting]: "It becomes blue-and-red; the attachment of the sorceress is dispelled. Her kinsmen prosper; may her husband be bound in bonds. (4)
One should honor that very guru. (5) This alone is the removal of the hair-tuft for young girls; here, too, it is the anointing. (6) Now follows the *puṃsavana* rite. (1)

When the months of pregnancy have mostly passed, one should cook three *sthālīpāka* offerings for Agni, Indra, and Viṣṇu. Of these, he offers oblations according to the respective deity: "Agni, most renowned," "O Indra, dominion," and "That Viṣṇu. He makes an additional offering with the verse: "A male indeed is Agni; a male is Indra; a male was Viṣṇu born. May he beget a male son, that he may bring forth a son in the tenth month. By whom, being born as a powerful one, we may live a hundred autumns and see a hundred autumns—grant us such a one, a giver of hundreds, a giver of thousands, a winner of cattle, a winner of horses, a hero, Svāhā! (2–3)
Now, regarding the *soṣyantī-savana* rite:

when she is about to give birth, he should place his hand, wet with water, upon her head and touch her from the heart, saying: "As this wind blows, as the ocean surges, so may your embryo stir; together with the afterbirth, let it fall away. Thus, she gives birth quickly.
When a son is born, a name is bestowed upon him:
it should consist of four syllables, beginning with a sonant (ghoṣavat) and an internal semi-vowel (antaḥstha),
or it may be formed according to what is appropriate.

Having brought fire and offered oblations in it up to the *ājyabhāga* portion, he should pour the remnants (*saṃpāta*) into a bronze vessel containing gold with two verses: "Hiraṇyagarbha," "The image of the year," "To Kāya svāhā," "To Ka svāhā," "To Katama svāhā," "To Prajāpati svāhā," and the two verses beginning with "O Prajāpati, for there is none other than you.

(4) Having made the mouth pure with gold according to the verse "Thou art the life of Agni," and having touched his mouth with water and washed his hands, he consecrates the breasts with three verses beginning with "Honey is the wind for the one who follows the Law," reciting them verse by verse, and both together with the last one. (5)

Having rubbed the *saṃpāta* residues together with gold—some say [adding] honey—and having placed that in his mouth, he makes him drink it, saying: "Suck up life; suck up old age; suck up truth; suck up prosperity; suck up vigor; suck up abundance of wealth; suck up the splendor of sacred knowledge.
Live for a hundred autumns; see for a hundred autumns. Having caused him to smell it on the head, he makes him recite the *svastyayana* (prayers for well-being).

He offers mustard seeds mixed with husks with a ladle, saying: "Śaṇḍa, Marka, Upavīta, Tauṇḍuleya, Ulūkhala, Capala—may they perish from here, Svāhā! Anālikhan, Avalikhan, Kiṃvadanta, Ulūkhala, Capala—may they perish from here, Svāhā! Haryakṣṇa, Kumbhi, Śakti, Hantṛ, Cupaṇīmukha, Capala—may they perish from here, Svāhā! Keśinī, Śvalominī, Kavakeśā, Avakāśinī—may they go away and perish from here, Svāhā!
In this manner he should offer oblations morning and evening for ten days.

On the tenth day, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (oblation of rice) in that same fire with milk, having bathed [the child] including the head with all kinds of perfumes and superior fruits, and having covered him with a new garment, he offers of the *sthālīpāka* with the two verses beginning "kayā naścitra" and "kayā tacchṛṇve," and with the two [verses] "prajāpataye svāhā" and "prajāpataye nahi tvad anya. 1. The procedure is the same up to the touching of the forehead with the formula "agnerāyur asi. 2.
That very name is bestowed [at this point]. 3.
Some say it is otherwise:

before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having poured purified clarified butter into a bronze vessel and placed a piece of gold—reciting "The life-span of Agni"—into it, he offers from it with the five verses beginning "The breath of Indra.
Before the *saṃsthitayajus*, the Brahman priest and all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) cast the gold into the clarified butter, reciting "As the serpent... and so forth.
Having lifted it up with the verse "By the purifying [Soma]," he hands it to the sacrificer with the formula, "The gods are long-lived.
7 He drinks that [mixture], having poured clarified butter from the gold vessel.
8 Having washed it, he fastens the gold [vessel] on [the sacrificer] with the verse, "O Agni, this [person]. 9

Having touched his forehead, he murmurs: "The breath of the Aśvins. Having smelled him on the head with the words: "From limb by limb you arise, from the heart you are born; you are indeed the self named son; live a hundred autumns, see a hundred autumns," he causes him to recite a benediction.
Thus it is after returning from a journey, and thus month by month, having offered the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, [he performs] the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) with clarified butter for one year.
They shall not eat meat for a year;
when the year is completed, having sacrificed with a goat and a sheep to Agni and Dhanvantari, he should feed the Brahmins food mixed with clarified butter.
On the third half-month, there is the sight of the sun.

On an auspicious day or on a festival, when the sun has risen, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a chariot wheel and having kindled the fire upon it as prescribed, he offers oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, and then offers clarified butter with the verses: "The crosser of heaven," "The golden disk," "Upwards that [sun]," and "The bright face of the gods.
(2) He offers the cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) with the verses: "Mitra [protects] the people" and "Him, Mitra, [the people].
(3) With the verse "Turn toward us," they lead the boy forward. (4)
The worship of the sun consists of the two [verses] "draṣṭre namaḥ" and "adṛśram asya";
one should feed Brāhmaṇas with food mixed with clarified butter.
Thus also for the sight of the moon. 1.5–6.1.
With the two verses, "Swiftly the Ordainer [is born] again," he makes an offering of four spoonfuls of clarified butter at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
With the two verses, "Swell up" and "May thy milks," he offers of the cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*).
With the verse, "New, ever new," he performs the reverential salutation (*upasthāna*).
The Dakṣiṇā is a light. 5.

In the sixth month, or when the teeth have appeared, the first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) takes place. Having mixed together all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), and having offered oblations with the verses, "O God, giver of life, whose face is ghee" (RV 1.91.8) and "Lord of food, of the food... (RV 1.187.1), he should cause the boy to eat the food with that very [second verse]. 2.
When the greater part of the third year has passed, he causes the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) to be performed: 1.
for the Vasiṣṭhas, on the right side; 2.
for the Atris and Kaśyapas, on both sides; 3. [and for others, on the top].
The Bhṛgus have shaven heads; the Aṅgirases have five topknots;
some [have] a tuft of hair.

For the sake of auspiciousness, others [perform this] for a peacock, or according to family custom (7), on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight or on a festival day, having prepared the fire as prescribed and offered oblations with the *jaya* and other formulas, he consecrates the warm water with the mantra: "The Savitṛ has come hither with the razor; O Vāyu, come with warm water! O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, being of one mind, shave [the hair] of King Soma, you who are wise" (8). (9)

"May all those that are warm and cold come together; may Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ, whose law is truth, grant their approval. He should pour [the water] over [the child] with the words: "O you who give moisture! O you who give life! "Moistening, O givers of moisture, givers of life, flow here; let them moisten him so that he may live, for long life and for splendor. (10)

At the right side of the hair-parting, having placed a blade of *darbha* grass between with the mantra, "O herb, protect him! and having applied the razor with the mantra, "O razor," he shaves with the mantra: "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ, the knower, shaved the hair of King Soma and Varuṇa, with that, O Brahmins, shave this [boy] today, so that he may be long-lived, reach old age, and live a full life, N.N.! With that wherewith Dhātṛ shaved the hair of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra for the sake of their life-span—with that, shave his hair for the sake of his life-span, for good renown, and for well-being! With that wherewith Pūṣan shaved the hair of Prajāpati, Agni, and Sūrya for the sake of their life-span—"

"By that [means], shave for his life, for good renown, and for well-being; by which he may live longer and see the sun for a long time. By that [means], shave for his life, for good renown, and for well-being"—with these mantras, one performs the darbha-blade shaving ceremony, moving clockwise in each direction. "O shaver, as you shave the hair with the well-fashioned razor that rolls over it, cleanse the head; do not deprive him of his life"—with this, he hands the iron razor to the barber for the shaving of the hair.

"May this luster not follow after your hair; may the Creator (Dhātṛ) likewise bestow it upon you. May Indra, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa bestow luster upon you"—with these words he consecrates [the hair] as it falls away.
(13) He collects the hairs being pulled out by friends into fresh cow-dung.

(14) "When King Varuṇa had his hair shorn, Soma, Dhātṛ, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and Agni found for them a manifold resting place between heaven and earth, seeking their welfare"—with these words he consecrates them as they are carried away toward the north-east. (15)
"Do not leave anything remaining," says the Śruti (16).
He gives a boon to the officiant (17).
He hands over the eyelash-fringe and the sesame-paste for the shaving of the hair (18).
"One should feed the Brāhmaṇas food with clarified butter" (19).
Thus ends the third chapter in the Gṛhyapañcikā on the Laugākṣi-sūtra.
Initiation for a Brāhmaṇa occurs in the seventh year. 1.
In the ninth year for a Kṣatriya; in the eleventh for a Vaiśya;
there is no transgression for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year, for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.

Having bathed and had his hair combed, and having established the fire as prescribed, he offers oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others. He consecrates the unwashed garment with the mantra: "The Revatīs have smoothed you; the Kṛttikās have fashioned you; the waters have stretched you out; the prayers have spun you; the goddesses have cleansed you. A thousand women have placed you around on all sides; eighty women have spun you in the middle. (5) He causes him to put it on with the mantra: "O goddesses, clothe this man for the sake of the divine Savitṛ, bestowing splendor upon him; make him live a hundred years so that he may live. (6)

"Go to old age; put on a garment; you have become full and a protector against curses. Live for a hundred abundant autumns, and clothe yourself in the nourishment of wealth. We place this Soma around [him] for great splendor and for hearing, so that it may lead him to old age, that he may long remain awake for hearing, and that he may long be awake within his hearing"—this is for a Brāhmaṇa. "We place this [Soma] around [him], O Indra, for strength and for great sovereignty."

"For that he may lead him to old age, that he may long watch over his dominion, that he may long watch over his dominion"—this is for a Kṣatriya. "We place this person around for life, for great prosperity, so that he may lead him to old age, that he may long watch over prosperity, that he may long watch over prosperity"—this is for a Vaiśya. "Thou hast put on this garment for well-being; become stout, a protector against curses. Live a hundred autumns with heroic sons, and as a powerful one, distribute riches while living"—with these words he consecrates the one who has put on the garment, and also with these two verses beginning, "In every endeavor, O youth, well-clad. (7)

Having brought fire around to the right, he makes [the student] step upon a stone with his right foot, saying: "Come, step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm. May all the gods grant you a life of a hundred autumns. (8) With the words: "I give my vow to your heart; let your mind follow my mind. With single-minded devotion, enjoy my word. May Bṛhaspati bind you to me," he strokes [the student] upward from the region of the navel with his hand. (9) Having consumed curd three times with the verse beginning "Dadhikrāvan," he causes [the student] to recite: "I have come to the state of a religious student (*brahmacarya*); initiate me. Then he causes him to recite: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. (10)

"Driving away ill-spoken words, purifying my pure color, she has come to me. Bestowing strength through out-breath and in-breath, this goddess, auspicious and fortunate, is my girdle. Guardian of the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), performer of austerity, slaying the demon, overcoming the enemy—O auspicious one, go around us on every side! O girdle, may we not harm your husband. "Born from Faith, arisen from austerity, you have become the sister of the seers who compose the mantras. As such, O girdle, move about me; bestow upon me austerity and sensory power. Saying this, he fastens the girdle while making him recite. (11)
He gives a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass to the Brāhmaṇa, a bowstring of murvā fiber to the Rājanya, and one of hempen thread to the Vaiśya.

Having made a knot with the formula, "Thou art the equalizer of the mind; thou art a divine knot; mayest thou not come loose," he causes [the student] to recite: "The eye of Mitra, supporting, for strength, splendor, glorious, firm, and prosperous; an unwearied garment, moving—this skin of the antelope, O vigorous one, I put on. He gives the skin of the black antelope to the Brāhmaṇa, that of the tiger to the Rājanya, and that of the ruru deer to the Vaiśya.

He causes him to worship the sun with the mantra beginning, "That eye... (VS 4.14). When asked, "What is your name? and when the salutation has been uttered, he replies, "I am so-and-so, sir" (VS 4.15). [The teacher says:

"In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand; so-and-so, I initiate you, so-and-so. Savitṛ has taken your hand; Agni is your teacher. Who initiates you? So-and-so. To whom do I entrust you? To whom are you a student? He replies: 'I am a student of Prāṇa. (VS 4.16)

I entrust you to Prajāpati. I entrust you to the god Savitṛ. I entrust you to Bṛhaspati, O [Name]! O god Savitṛ, this is your student; protect him. May he live long; may he not die. He is the son of Agni. He is the son of Vāyu. He is the son of Sūrya. He is the son of Viṣṇu. He is the son of Brahmā. This is your student; protect him. May he live long; may he not die. You are a student (*brahmacārin*). Drink water. Perform your duties. Do not sleep during the day. Restrain your speech. 17

He causes [the student] to recite: "May wisdom come to me. "May the Aṅgirases give me wisdom; may the Seven Seers give me wisdom. May Agni and Vāyu, and may Dhātṛ, grant me wisdom. May King Varuṇa grant me wisdom; may Agni grant me wisdom. May Indra and Sūrya grant me wisdom; may the goddess Sarasvatī grant me wisdom. That wisdom which is among the Apsarases and that mind which is among the Gandharvas—the divine wisdom that is in man—may it enter into me here. May my body be discerning; may my speech yield sweetness."

"Listen to what has been heard by me; may I be able to remember that which has been recited to me. May we be dear to sacred learning; may we be endowed with wisdom. I have grown, and you have grown, O gentle one; you are my vital breath. Protect me! You two are the poles of the Veda; may what I have heard not be lost. (18) With these very four verses he should offer oblations for the study of the Vedas (*anupravacanīya*). With the last verse, "To the meters, svāhā!", he should offer using the name of the specific Veda; just as the sacrifice is performed according to its designation, so it is with all the declarations of the Vedas. (19)

To the west of the fire, seated on *darbha* grass facing east, he recites the *Sāvitrī* verse three times—first quarter by quarter, then hemistich by hemistich, and finally the whole verse—to one who is seated facing west; and also to anyone else who desires wisdom.

Having anointed a single-jointed staff made of *pālāśa* wood with fresh butter, he makes him recite while it is in the shade: "O you of good fame, you are of good fame; as you are of good fame, so make me of good fame and of good lineage. As you are of good fame among the gods, the guardian of the treasure of the Veda, so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Brahman and the Veda among the Brāhmaṇas."
He gives a staff of *pālāśa* wood to a Brāhmaṇa, one of *aśvattha* wood to a Rājanya, and one of *naiyagrodha* wood to a Vaiśya.

Then he makes him recite: "Remembered by me and not remembered by me—this is my twofold vow. Censure by me and non-censure by me—this is my twofold vow. Knowledge by me and ignorance by me—this is my twofold vow. Faith by me and lack of faith by me—this is my twofold vow. Truth by me and untruth by me—this is my twofold vow. Mortality by me and immortality by me—this is my twofold vow."

What has been heard by me and what has not been heard by me—that is my vow of both. What is the vow for me and what is the non-vow for me—that is my vow of both. That which is the vow of the Brāhmaṇa in his Brahman-nature; that which is the vow of Agni, together with Indra, Prajāpati, the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and men; together with the royal Kṣatriyas among men; together with the Gandharvas and Apsarases, and the other crawling creatures; together with the plants and trees; together with domestic and wild animals; together with the ether and the light.

"Whatever vow of mine is within my own self, together with its light and its radiance—that is my all-encompassing vow. Here I place this fuel upon the fire; O Agni, may I become one who observes the all-encompassing vow.
(23) "He who initiates one who knows thus studies one, two, three, or all of these Vedas," so says the Śruti. (24) He gives a gift to the officiant. (25)
One should conclude the remainder of the day. 26.
Celibacy has been explained. 27.
The Traividyaka [rite]. 1.
The rule for the teacher:
he who studies the Veda should place fuel-sticks on the fire with the *aṃhomuk* verses both before and after [the study].
The procedure for undertaking and releasing the vow has been stated.
Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the four officiating priests (*cāturhautṛka*).
1. He undertakes the vow according to the rule for a Vedic student (*brahmacārin*). 2. For one year, or eight months, or four months. 3.

On an auspicious day or on a festival day of the bright fortnight, having established the fire as prescribed and offered oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, he should drive a bunch of *darbha* grass into the ground to the east of the fire, seat a Brāhmaṇa to the south, and place fuel sticks upon the fire while reciting the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ.
(4) In the case of the regular undertaking of a vow, the fourth [verse], "O Brāhmaṇas, lords of vows," is used.

(5) Then, for the vow-oblations, one who desires splendor should use clarified butter with the *caturhotṛ* formulas; one desiring cattle, barley-gruel (*yāvaka*); one desiring vigor, food; and one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in milk. (6)
He recites a mantra over each oblation as it is offered mentally.
7. That which is the Vedic vow is the vow here.
8. We shall enumerate the modifications: one should not sit with four, nor eat in the presence of four, nor eat together with four, or even with one of them. 9.
Thus, at the conclusion [of the vow],
he gives a dwelling as a choice gift to the teacher seated to the south;
or, in the sixteenth year, the Godāna ceremony is performed when the fire ritual is completed.
This has been explained by the *jātakarman* (birth-rite).

Seated upon *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* grass, he sprinkles [the child] with gold and with water using two verses beginning with "The waters that are divine" (*yā āpo divyāḥ*)—either those used for the fire-rituals or those used for the *rājasūya*.
In this same manner, he sprinkles the king with the anuvāka beginning with "Impel him, O God" (*sāvīr hi deva*), according to the stated procedure for the non-deprivation of power (*akratvajyāni*).

Having mixed all the food fit for oblation with milk and water using the *anuvāka* beginning with "pitun nu stoṣam," he offers it with a ladle (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood, and also with the fourteen verses beginning with "vājasya nu prasava.

(5) That which he does not offer, he sprinkles upon the fuel-stick (*idhma*) of the *āgnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice; having poured the remainder as water, he sprinkles [the sacrificer] with that. (6) Now follows the restoration of the single fire (*ekāgni*). (1)
Upon the death of the *parameṣṭhin*, the son shall prepare the fire;
he shall cause everyone to fast;
he shall kindle that fire until the time of dawn.

One should pacify the fire with a mash of beans and grain using a cup made of udumbara wood, [reciting]: "We invoke Savitṛ the golden-handed, Vāyu, Indra, Prajāpati, and the divine Aṅgirases; may they pacify this flesh-eating Agni.

(5) Having gathered the ashes in a mat woven of kāśa grass, one should cast them away [with the words]: "I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of Yama, carrying off the impurity. Let this other Jātavedas here carry the oblation to the gods, knowing [the way]. (6)

Saying, "It is burnt," they place it at a crossroads in the south-western direction; upon that [spot], they perform the purification over a pillow and a lead weight with the verse: "We wipe away the thieves from the lead and from the pillow with the head. Having wiped away the flesh-eater along with them, go forth, O bounteous ones! (7)

Having worshipped with the four verses beginning "Go away from here" (*apāsmat etu*), and having touched water with the verse "May the goddesses be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*), they return against the current and disturb the footprints with reeds or a branch of cane, thinking, "Disturbing the footprint of Death. [They say: "Disturbing the footprint of Death, may we, gaining a longer life, increase in offspring and wealth; being pure and purified, may you become worthy of sacrifice. (8) Right there they should deposit the branch. (9)

"Placing the ox in front, they go forth; the ox is the boat. "Grasp the ox, the boat; may it carry you across all misfortunes. Ascend Savitṛ’s golden boat; with six waves may we cross over to immortality.

Having returned and touched the smokeless smoke, they circumambulate the fire three times to the right with a cow and the fire, reciting: "They have led the cow around; they have carried the fire around. They have established glory among the gods; who shall dare to attack them? "They have led the cow around; they have carried the fire around. They have established glory among the gods; who shall dare to attack them? (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.5.10–11)

Having placed a stone and gold in a water-pot, they then touch those [stones] with the verse, "The stony one flows" (*aśmanvatī*). "The stony one flows; take hold of each other, arise, and move forward, O friends! Here we leave behind those who were unkind; may we cross over toward auspicious strengths.
Having become pure, he should offer [the food] to the ancestors.
Having eaten the *aupavastra* meal, he should bring fire from somewhere, keep it burning, and lie down near it.
In the Upakāśa and Upaśānta [fires], having removed the ashes and having scattered the earthen materials with the first [verse],
he arranges them with the second [verse].

Having produced another fire-brand in the same manner as it was previously produced, he holds it at the height of the knees and places it with the formula, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ, O Aṅgirases," and with "O good Gārhapatya. [He continues: "O good Gārhapatya, driving away our enemies, make each dawn for us more auspicious than the last. For long life lasting a hundred autumns, bestow upon us great fortune!
Having placed the wooden fuel-sticks together with gold, [he performs the rite].
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with [the verse] beginning with "tulyena," he should sacrifice with an *āgneya* cooked rice offering (*sthālīpāka*) or with an animal victim.
A cow, a garment, a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*), and gold are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
This fire is either the *aupāsada* or the nuptial fire.

The Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt formulas; the two Vārtraghna Ājyabhāgas;

One should worship the deity by name; for that deity, one should recite a verse addressed to Agni, or one addressed to Agni-Soma, or one addressed to Indra-Agni among those deities shared by two gods, or one addressed to the Viśvedevas among those shared by many gods (11).

One should offer oblations with the two verses beginning "Thou, O Agni, for us... and with the formula "Earth! Bhūḥ!", as well as all the expiations (prāyaścittas) with the seven verses beginning "The mind is the light...
(14). One should throw the sacrificial grass coverings (paristaraṇa) into the fire; however, some say one should not throw them in (15).

In sacrifices performed under the constellations (*nakṣatra-yajña*), one should sacrifice with the *ṛc*-verses dedicated to the deities of those constellations: "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*); "Hiraṇyagarbha" (*hiraṇyagarbhaḥ*); "O Maruts, that which... "Varuṇa has approached with his coils like a serpent; may Pūṣan follow our cows; Yama bestows your wondrous deeds"—with these verses, one verse at a time (he should offer).

Now follows the Śūlagava sacrifice:

Having fashioned a sacrificial altar (vedi) in the shape of a cow in the midst of cows or to the north of the village, and having surrounded it with branches, they erect a hewn sacrificial post (yūpa) silently.

To the west of that, having kindled the fire as previously described and offered oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, he dedicates either a cow or a beast to Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Īśvara, Paśupati, and Adhipati.

Having silently prepared six *puroḍāśa* cakes on single potsherds—one for each name, one for each *dru* (tree), and one for each *anuvāka*—and having arranged six offerings of red meat in vessels or on *darbha* grass before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he worships with the six *anuvākas* beginning with "Homage to you, O Rudra, in your wrath," and he attaches the verse "Thee, the Lord, the tearer" (*īśānaṃ tvā śśruma*) everywhere.
(7) They feed a large number of Brahmins. (8) They do not allow raw meat to enter the village. (9)

One should offer oblations in the *aupāsada* fire to the deities of the morning and evening *agnihotra*.
On the festival day, having fasted with his wife, he should offer oblations to the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
he should offer additional oblations with clarified butter to the deities of the first-fruits sacrifice;
the consecration of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering and the consumption [of the remnants] have already been explained.

When the Vaiśvadeva food has been prepared—the finest of all—he offers oblations to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Indra-Agni, the Viśve Devas, Prajāpati, Anumati, Dhānvantari, Vāstoṣpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
(He offers) to Takṣa and Upatakṣa on both sides.
To the east of the fire, he offers seven oblations with the formula beginning, "Thou art Ambā by name."
To the domestic deities, he says, "O Nandinī, O Subhagā, O Sumaṅgalī, grant auspiciousness," while moving clockwise around the corners.
To the pillar, to Dhruvā, to Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī, and to the lords of the forest (Vanaspati), [he offers].
At the door of Dharma and Adharma, and to Mṛtyu, [he offers].
"To Varuṇa, the receptacle," [he offers] on the mortar; "To Viṣṇu," on the pestle;

He places the remaining rice-balls for the ancestors.
Having set down a water-pitcher, he causes [the officiant] to recite a prayer for well-being.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Gṛhyapañcikā on the Laugākṣi-sūtra.

Now follow the seasonal *svastyayana* (rites for well-being). On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, he should set out four oblations: a cake (*apūpa*), a cooked mess of grain (*sthālīpāka*), parched grains (*dhānāḥ*), groats (*saktavaḥ*), and both [the parched grains and groats] of unbroken rice.

He offers the cake with the verse, "O Viṣṇu, homage to thee! (RV 7.99.1); the cooked mess of grain with the verse, "The night has shone forth" (RV 10.127.1); the parched grains with the verse, "Homage be to the serpents" (AV 5.13.1); and the groats with the verse, "Those who... eat" (AV 2.24.1).
Or, in the holes where there are "sorcerers" (yātudhāna), he should offer groats with a ladle;
in both cases, he should present an offering to the King of Mice (akhurāja), either at the beginning and the end, or at both times.

When a pigeon has alighted on the fire-enclosure and, being distressed by fear, leaves its footprint in the groats or in the ashes, he offers a portion of cooked rice (sthālīpāka) with the eight-verse hymn beginning, "The god, the pigeon... (devaḥ kapotaḥ).
"Let them lead a cow around here," they say, and they lead a cow around [the fire];
that is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
On the full moon day of Āśvayuja, they honor the horses and all the draft animals.

To the north of the village, having fashioned a site in the shape of an altar (vedi) and surrounded it with branches, one should fill jars with all kinds of liquids and place them in the cardinal directions, and vessels with all kinds of seeds in the intermediate directions. To the west of that, having kindled the fire as previously described and offered oblations with the *jaya* and other formulas, one should worship the three deities: Varuṇa, Agni, the two Aśvins, and the month of Āśvayuja.
While the sacrifice is being performed, they yoke the horses and all the draft animals.
Wearing their armor, they circumambulate the sacrificial ground three times from left to right;
they express their joy;
and once the sacrifice is completed, they depart as they please.
A cow, clothing, bronze, and gold are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). 8.

On the full moon day of Kārttika, or under the asterism Revatī of the month of Āśvayuja, having kindled a well-kindled fire in the midst of cows and having cooked a *caru* offering for Pūṣan in milk, he offers the portion of Pūṣan with the mantra: "May Pūṣan follow after our cows" (RV 6.58.1). Having offered with "May there be prosperity here" (RV 7.54.1), and having murmured the Rudra-hymn.

"Whosoever would cover the herd of a cow that has a living calf and is full of milk—whether her son be of one form or two forms—and who is the most radiant in the herd: having adorned him, and having adorned four or eight heifers, I give this young man to you as a husband; sport with him, your beloved, and roam about. May we not be deprived of offspring nor of our bodies; may we not come to harm for the sake of the enemy, O King Soma! (5)

Having spread out a covering with its fringes pointing northward, having placed water at the head of the bed, and having scattered rice and barley, he sprinkles the bed with water while reciting the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses; then, with the verse "Indra is the protector," he sweeps the bed with a branch of the *Śamī* tree.
Having put on an unwashed garment with the verse "The armor of Indra and Agni," he lies down on his right side with the verse "Gentle is the earth," ending with the word "luminous.
This sequence, beginning from the sprinkling and ending with the lying down, is repeated a second time.
On the full moon day of Caitra, there is the *udrohaṇa* [of the sacrificial post]; there is no bed above, nor is there a *sthālīpāka* offering here, nor does he wipe with a branch.

He should make the pieces of meat at the sites for the excision red-hot with charcoal;

Having scattered sesame seeds on all sides with the two verses beginning "May the Asuras depart," and having murmured the verses beginning "Come here, O Fathers" and "O Fathers, come to me; may they disappear behind the mountains," he should bring water for the feet for the odd-numbered [ancestors] with the verse beginning "Those who stand there, immortal speech" and "She who is my mother."
And he should bring water with these very [verses];
having looked at these [deities]— the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus—

(9), he touches the prepared food with the three verses beginning, "Those who are my fathers, this is for you, O fathers; this is the sacrifice" (10), and having poured milk or ghee over it with the verse, "This is your strength; within these [foods] is the cooked [essence]" (11).
Having addressed [the offerings] according to their respective gender with the formulas, "Svadhā, obeisance to such-and-such; svadhā, obeisance to such-and-such," he should cause them to eat.

Having said, "May you eat," and having looked at those who are eating with the formula, "Whatever I have done out of desire," and with these [other verses], "O flesh-eaters, by means of days and nights, carry the svadhā for you," he should perform the pouring down [of the remnants] with the formula, "The earth is the ladle."
With the words, "O fathers who have passed away here," he should lay down the garments;
with the verse, "Carrying strength," he should sprinkle water around;
and with the verse, "May it not fail me," he should sprinkle food together with grass.
Having brought the food that is free from poison, and having said, "Is it complete? and "May you be satisfied," [he asks] "Are you satisfied? 18.
Having had them rinse their mouths after they are satisfied, and having performed a circumambulation while reciting "yan me rāma," 19.
having returned and said, "May you take pleasure," he worships with the remainder of the section beginning "devāś ca pitaraś ca. 20.

Having spread the fires over them and sprinkled them with water, he strews *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward.

Following the procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, having placed [the portions] upon the three eastern mounds and having poured marrow over them, he sprinkles them all around with milk. Having said, "Whatever essences (*rasa*) may be here, let these be for you," and having said, "May you be satisfied," [he concludes].

In the same manner, he should give liquor—excluding the marrow—to the other women. Now, the rule for the first *śrāddha* has been explained by that of the *aṣṭakā*.

The procedure for the disposal [of the remnants] has been explained previously. Now, on the full moon day of Phālguna, he offers an oblation of oil-cakes with the verse, "Aryaman is the deity; those [cakes] of yours, O Aryaman... (RV 5.2.4). 1–2.
Then he offers the *indrāṇī* oblations with the verse "prasasāhiṣe" (RV 10.180.2) for the *tuṇḍila* grains;

With the two verses, "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is Indra's wife," one offers of two rice-messes mixed with vegetables and sesame paste (6).
With the two verses, "The cows are Bhaga," one performs the cow-sacrifice (1). With the three verses beginning, "They yoke the ploughs," one performs the rite of yoking the plough (2).
He joins [the oxen] with the first and the last [yokes], and with the middle one he joins the ploughshare.
With the formula, "O good ploughshares," he ploughs two furrows, moving from left to right.

"yā oṣadhayaḥ" (those herbs which) is for the rite of sowing seed.

thus for the first sowing.

For the sake of pacification when a portent or a marvel occurs, he mixes together—using the formula "I mix you"—the *śamī* wood, the *śamuka*, the *śāmyavāka*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *udumbara* wood, *dūrvā* grass, six blades of *darbha* grass with tips pointing eastward, *sumanas* flowers, *apāmārga*, all kinds of seeds, a clod of earth from a furrow, cow dung, gold, and the mound of an anthill, along with water, using the two verses beginning "I mix you.

With the eight-verse hymn beginning "O gods, whatever fear we have from portents," he offers oblations of *sthālīpāka*; with the three verses beginning "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods," with the four verses beginning "May it be auspicious for our ears," and with the verse "The armor of Indra and Agni"—the sprinkling has been explained.
Having offered oblations with the *dhūr* and *upadhūr* verses, there is again a sprinkling.
